origin: Dry rocky slopes of Iraq, Iran and the southern Caucasus Mountains
habitat: Stony, gritty alpine and sub-alpine slopes and screes in full sun
blurb: A true wild lamb's-ear species rather than a garden selection, and the closest thing the genus offers to a flowering counterpart of the familiar silver mat. It builds a low, tufted, woody-based cushion of narrow grey-green leaves — lavender-like in outline, which is where the name comes from — and then in May and June throws short spikes wrapped in a shaggy cotton-wool calyx from which lavender-pink flowers poke out. Missouri Botanical Garden files it under 'lamb's ears' and 'pink cotton lamb's ear' for exactly that reason. An alpine from the dry mountains of Iran and the Caucasus, it is built for lean, gritty ground and hard sun, which makes it a natural rock-garden and trough plant on the Front Range — but it wants the sharp drainage of its home scree, not a watered border.
sun: Full sun; tolerates some light shade
water: Low; xeric once established — needs sharp drainage and resents wet, humid ground
spread: A tufted, woody-based clump creeping slowly by stolons into a small-scale patch; well-behaved, not a takeover artist
seasons: Grey-green tufted cushion through the growing season; cottony lavender-pink flower spikes in late spring and early summer; dies back to a low tuft over winter
wildlife: Bees work the lavender-pink flowers, as they do the rest of the mint family; the grey foliage is left alone by browsers
deer: Deer resistant — the aromatic grey foliage is not browsed
toxic: No toxicity on record; the dried flowering tops are brewed as a traditional Iranian herbal tea, but this is a folk-medicinal rather than culinary plant
gaps: Reel is spring- and early-summer-only. This is a wild Iranian/Caucasian alpine with only a few dozen CC-licensed photos worldwide, nearly all taken in the May–June flowering window by hikers; no open-licensed fall, winter or seedhead shot exists. Capped at good for the seasonal axis.

care.hardiness: Winter hardy in USDA zones 5–8, which puts the Front Range (zones 5b–6a) inside its range but near the cold edge, so site it somewhere with good winter drainage rather than a low spot that collects snowmelt.[1] It is an alpine from the dry rocky slopes of Iraq, Iran and the southern Caucasus, so cold is not what troubles it — wet is.[1] Our dry winters and lean soils suit it considerably better than a mild, damp climate would.
care.planting: Plant in spring after the soil warms, or in early fall to let the roots take hold before freeze-up; mid-May and early September are the usual Front Range windows.[3] Plant it high, on a slope, a berm or the shoulder of a rock, and top-dress with gravel rather than bark so the crown stays dry. It is well suited to containers and troughs, where you can guarantee the drainage — but a pot freezes and dries far faster than open ground, so use a gritty alpine mix and tuck the pot somewhere sheltered for winter.[1]
care.sun: Full sun.[1] It tolerates some light shade, but shade costs it the tight cushion habit and keeps the foliage damp, which is how an alpine like this gets into trouble.[1]
care.soil: Dry to medium-moisture, well-drained soil, and it performs especially well in gritty, rocky substrates — this is a rock-garden plant by temperament.[1] It takes the neutral-to-alkaline range that Front Range soils sit in, roughly pH 6.0–8.0.[1] If your ground is heavy clay, do not try to amend it into submission; build a raised gritty pocket or grow it in a trough instead.
care.water: Dry to medium.[1] Water it through its first season to establish, then leave it largely alone — deep, infrequent soaks in a long drought are far better than regular sprinkling. Water at the base; the cottony flower spikes and hairy leaves hold overhead water, and standing moisture on the crown in hot weather is what brings on rot.[1]
care.spacing: Set plants 12–18 in apart when using it as a small-scale groundcover.[1] Give it room for air to move around the cushion, especially in a sheltered bed.
care.propagation: Divide the tufted, woody-based clumps in spring, teasing off rooted stoloniferous pieces from the outside of the cushion and replanting them immediately in gritty soil.[1] It can also be raised from seed sown in a gritty mix, and basal cuttings taken in late spring root readily — but division is the simplest and gives a usable plant fastest. Replant divisions high, with the crown proud of the surface.
care.bloom: Lavender-to-pink flowers, each about ¾ in long, open on erect stems in May and June, sitting in a dense woolly calyx that gives the whole spike a cottony look and holds its interest after the flowers themselves have gone.[1] It is a spring-into-early-summer bloomer rather than a long-season one; do not expect the all-summer performance of a border perennial.
care.feeding: None needed, and none advised. This is a lean-soil alpine; feeding produces soft, sprawling growth that flops and rots.
care.maintenance: Genuinely low maintenance.[1] Deadhead the spent flower spikes once they have gone over — it improves the plant's appearance and helps maintain its vigour.[1] Tidy winter-damaged foliage out of the cushion in early spring, and keep gravel rather than damp mulch around the crown. Lift and divide every few years if the middle of the cushion opens up.
care.troubles: The real risks are all moisture-related: leaf spots, powdery mildew and rot in hot, humid summers, plus slugs and snails sheltering under the cushion.[1] Boulder's dry summer air makes all of these far less likely than they would be in the East — but a drip line running under the foliage or a lawn sprinkler clipping the bed will re-create the problem. Sharp drainage and base watering solve nearly everything that goes wrong with this plant.
care.companions: A natural for rock gardens, wildflower plantings, border edging, small-scale groundcover and trough or container culture.[1] It sits well with other lean-soil, sharp-drainage plants — dianthus, sedums, small penstemons and thymes — and the grey cushion and cottony spikes contrast nicely with the flat silver of the ordinary lamb's ears.

edible.summary: The dried flowering tops are brewed as a traditional herbal tea in Iran, but that is a folk-medicinal preparation, not a culinary food — don't treat it as a kitchen herb.[2][4]
edible.caution: Stachys lavandulifolia is not a food plant and is not listed here as one. In Iran the flowering aerial parts are traditionally steeped as a herbal tea to settle gastrointestinal complaints, and the extract has a folk reputation as a mild sedative and anti-anxiety remedy.[2][4] That is a medicinal tradition, not a vegetable or a culinary herb, and the record is one of traditional use plus animal-model pharmacology rather than tested human safety: the aerial parts carry a mix of flavonoids, an iridoid and a labdane diterpenoid whose effects have been studied in the laboratory, but no safe dose, drug interaction profile or safety in pregnancy has been established.[2] Do not eat the leaves as a green, do not assume the tea tradition transfers to any other Stachys in this guide, and do not use it medicinally without proper advice — grow it as the handsome alpine groundcover it is.
